USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture — keep List 3 in place as scheduled (10% now, rising to 25% on Jan 1, 2019) to keep pressure on Beijing, and keep the negotiating window open, but do not trigger a further escalation round (the threatened ~$267B List 4) or pull the Jan 1 increase forward before judging China's response. Do not make unilateral concessions either; the leverage is ours to keep.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The dispute state reads as a mild opportunity for the US, not a threat: the U.S. economy is robust (industrial production index rising to 104.1, consumer sentiment at 100.1, 10Y yield 3.06%, broad dollar strong near 113.7), and the US holds the structural upper hand — tariff coverage of ~$250B (half of Chinese imports) with a credible path to cover essentially everything China ships, while China, importing far fewer US goods, cannot fully retaliate in kind; market consensus is that the US is 'winning so far' (Forbes 2018-08-23, NYT 2018-09-17). That justifies a slightly negative threat score. However, the reason to hold rather than escalate further is domestic and second-order: China is retaliating on soybeans and other farm products concentrated in electorally decisive states weeks before the November midterms, GOP members (e.g., Ways & Means chair Brady; Sen. Heitkamp) call the tariffs a tax on US consumers, and pushing the $200B round to 25% now or triggering List 4 would raise consumer prices at peak holiday-shipping season and add market volatility. With China signaling it may decline serious talks until after the midterms, the disciplined move is to hold the course already set and remain available for negotiation — neither over-escalating nor conceding.
key_factors: US holds initiative and leverage (~$250B coverage, credible path to cover all Chinese imports; China can't fully retaliate in kind)
US economy strong and unaffected so far (IP 104.1, sentiment 100.1, 10Y 3.06%, dollar 113.7)
List 3 effective Sept 24 at 10%, scheduled to rise to 25% Jan 1 2019 — pressure already in motion
China retaliation on soybeans/farm products hitting electorally vital states before Nov midterms
GOP criticism that tariffs are a consumer tax; risk of further escalation raising consumer prices near holidays
China may decline serious talks until after midterms — hold and keep negotiation window open

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain our existing proportional retaliation as leverage but hold the line and actively pursue a negotiated de-escalation ahead of the G20 window — do not escalate further, and do not concede on core structural/tech-transfer demands. We have already responded to each US round (34bn, 16bn, and now $60bn at 5-10%), so adding more would only feed an asymmetric spiral where the US is covering ~$250bn of our exports and threatens ~$267bn more. Instead, keep channels open, signal readiness for talks, and brace the economy with stimulus/fx-management while the scheduled January 2019 hike to 25% on $200bn hangs over us.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high but not existential. The timeline shows the US escalating at every step despite the May truce: List 3 took effect Sept 24 at 10% on ~$200bn (~$250bn total Section 301 coverage), with a scheduled rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019 (2018-09-17/24 entries), and Trump has threatened Phase 3 (~$267bn more, nearly all our exports). Firm-level targeting is already live (ZTE denial order, Apr 16). Macro evidence confirms strain: the yuan has depreciated ~9% since April, and economists project a 0.5-0.6ppt GDP drag in 2019 if tariffs go to 25%, with China taking a roughly four-times-larger hit than the US given our export exposure. That is high threat, warranting a score around +0.5. However, escalation is the wrong lever: US goods exports to China (~$130bn) give Beijing far less symmetric latitude to retaliate (analysts and Ross note we are running low on US products to target), so further escalation would hurt us more than them and hand the US cover for the January 2025 rate hike. The disciplined response to a high, structurally asymmetric threat is therefore to hold our measured retaliation, keep negotiating (Beijing has already framed its tariffs as defensive, 5-10%, and reiterated willingness for 'constructive dialogue'), and de-escalate rather than mirror-escalate. This justifies a neutral action stance: no new escalation, no concession on core demands.
key_factors: US Section 301 coverage now ~$250bn, with $200bn at 10% rising to 25% Jan 1, 2019
Trump threat of Phase 3 (~$267bn) covering virtually all Chinese exports
China retaliation capped at $60bn (5-10%) vs US 10-25% on $200bn - asymmetric capacity
Yuan down ~9% since April; projected 0.5-0.6ppt GDP drag in 2019
ZTE denial order shows firm-level/tech targeting already active
May 2018 truce collapsed - repeated US escalation despite talks
